Yes, we should raise the minimum wage.
We have recently seen that the UK is suffering from a cost of living crisis and that inflation is at a staggering rate. We have also seen that wages are stagnating, not rising at the same rate that the cost of living is rising, making it harder for people to provide for themselves. Therefore, the minimum wage should be raised to reflect this.
There is a problem with income disparity in the UK today. The minimum wage should be raised to ensure that the gap is closed.

We have also seen that wages are stagnating, not rising at the same rate that the cost of living is rising, making it harder for people to provide for themselves. Therefore, the minimum wage should be raised to reflect this.
There is a problem with income disparity in the UK today. The minimum wage should be raised to ensure that the gap is closed. This should be done for all age groups, to ensure that the younger and older generations are not being exploited, and that they can provide for themselves in their old age.
The minimum wage should be raised above the state benefits available in order to encourage people to work. It is important to create an incentive to work, as otherwise it can create a culture of benefits dependency.

We should raise the minimum wage in the UK. However, this should be done gradually over time. The price of everything is going up and up and up, however the minimum wage has risen but no where near inline with the cost of living making it harder and harder for people on minimum wage to continue affording basic necessities let alone luxuries. Raising the minimum wage will allow those working in lower paid roles some more of the opportunities that those earning aa higher wage have. These opportunities can be through experiences or just the security and reassurance they can pay their bills. However, it is important to support the living standards of our lowest-paid workers at a time when they too are feeling increased pressure from a rising cost of living. It is also important to support the employment of those with learning difficulties and criminal records etc.

It is important to provide people with a fair minimum wage so they do not need to rely on the state benefit system in order to survive. Minimum wage is not the same as a living wage - which would be ideal, but which is difficult to achieve for many employers working in difficult trading conditions. Minimum wages support those in the unskilled labour market and ensure that employers pay a fair wage and don't exploit their employees. However, raising the minimum wage would also cause prices to rise, putting extra strain on the finances of many businesses. Also, by raising the minimum wage, this would create a significant difference between the income of low wage earners and those who have skills, education and expertise and are able to earn more than minimum wage.

I believe that we should raise the minimum wage in the UK. I think that the current minimum wage is too low to be practical in today’s society. The cost of living has risen too much resulting in a lower standard of living and no longer incentivises work. Many people do not get what they need to live decently. The current minimum wage is too low compared to CPI and inflation. This could also prevent industrial actions in the future. This could provide a much needed boost to the economy as people now have less disposable income and many businesses have suffered as a result. Many people in work are having to claim top up benefits or even use food banks to make ends meet which is shocking - if someone works they should not be struggling to make enough money to feed themselves or their family! If we raise the minimum wage, it will help people to survive and it will be good for the economy. People will be able to buy more things and this will increase sales in shops and supermarkets. This will help the economy to grow. The cost of living crisis makes it very hard to survive on the minimum wage. It is only fair that we increase it.

Yes, we should raise the minimum wage in the UK. We need to help those on the lowest incomes to cope with the high cost of living. This will be good for the economy as people will have more money to spend. Businesses will need to absorb the cost of the increase, but this will be offset by the increased spending in the economy. We also need to increase the living wage to a level that people can live on without relying on benefits. This will reduce the welfare bill and increase tax revenues, which will help the economy. We also need to stop age-grading the minimum wage, as it is unfair that young people are paid less for doing the same job as adults.

Yes, we should raise the minimum wage in the UK, but we need to help those on the lowest incomes. We also need to make sure businesses are able to afford an increase, as many are already struggling. Increasing the minimum wage alone will not be sufficient, as people will just need to pay for the higher living costs, and businesses will pass this on. We need to simultaneously make welfare reform, encouraging people to work and making it financially sensible. Raising the minimum wage will help with this. We also need to increase the living wage to a level that people can live on without relying on benefits. This will reduce the welfare bill and increase tax revenues, which will help the economy. We also need to stop age-grading the minimum wage, as it is unfair that young people are paid less for doing the same job as adults. This change in policy will help young people into the workplace, stimulate the economy, and reduce the welfare bill.

Yes. We should raise the minimum wage in the UK. There are so many people who are struggling with basic costs of living who work full time. We are one of the richest countries in the world, people should be able to live a good life when they are working a full time job. We also believe that the disparity between the minimum wage and the average wage is too great and the minimum wage has not risen in line with the cost of living. There are no concrete disadvantages to raising the minimum wage. There are plenty of high-level earner who would not feel the pinch of higher taxation. Equally, raising minimum wage should not mean a reduction of benefits, whether from the government or from a particular job post.

We think that the government should also be looking at other ways to help the least well off in society such as tax credits and benefits. We should raise the minimum wage in the UK. There is a cost of living crisis in the UK, with inflation reaching up to 10%. The minimum wage should reflect this. The current government is more than happy to pour money into business instead of the public. The bottom line here is that "work should pay". This means that someone should be able to live solely on their income from a full-time minimum wage in the UK without also having to rely on in-work benefits from the government just to be able to live out a meagre existence. The cost of living crisis should have brought this into sharp focus, where many more individuals and families have struggled with everyday costs. The triple-lock on pensions allows for inflationary increases on retirement benefits, why not have parity with minimum wage? Countries that are more equal have been shown to have better outcomes across a wide range of measures.

We believe that the minimum wage should be raised in the UK. We feel that the cost of living is rising for all and that many on the minimum wage have to work long hours in order to earn enough to survive on. This reduces quality family time, leisure time and increases pressure. Subsequently this will have an immense effect on mental health, physical health and relationships. This will then impact on current services in place to support these matters. We feel that a higher minimum wage should be paid but not on the understanding that all wages rise. It should be paid to try to address some of the issues of inequality which are so great in the UK. Many of the recipients of minimum wage are the youngest in society and we feel that they are already discriminated in many ways. Paying them more would be a step in the right direction. We feel also that minimum wage differentials should be closed so that the discrepancy between minimum wage for different age groups are closed. We feel that lower paid workers should receive a raise. Particularly the care industry. They deserve a much higher rate of pay. This would encourage better work standards and improve the workers standard of living.

It is also important that people are not reliant on benefits to survive. It is also important that people are not reliant on benefits to survive. Raising the minimum wage would help to reduce the gap between the rich and the poor. It would also help to reduce the reliance on in work benefits. It would also encourage more people to apply for and remain in lower paid, often crucial roles that are the backbone of our society. The minimum wage should be enough for someone working full time (40 hours per week) to live on. You should be able to afford housing, food and some savings when working for minimum wage and only need one employment. To have anything under this benefits only those paying wages as the government have to subsidise those not earning enough. When a big company pays poverty wages and posts millions of pounds in profit that is not useful to the general public. 
There could be different levels depending on employers and ages but the minimum wage is ridiculously low versus the cost of living.

We should raise the minimum wage in order to incentivise people to be more efficient in their working habits as they would feel more valued. The minimum wage isn't enough for people to live on, especially in cities like London. Also, it will incentivise people to work -- what's the point in trying to find work when you won't earn enough to live on? We are falling behind inflation and companies should be made to provide a decent minimum wage with help from the government. We should raise the minimum wage in the UK. This is because the cost of living has increased above the rate of inflation, the means to live i.e. being paid - should also be increased too. This would be an incentive for more people to try and find employment instead of claiming benefits. Also, at present, minimum wage does not sufficiently cover what it costs to live in this country. That should be the measure, if you are on minimum wage, you should be able afford housing, electricity/gas, food and any other basic necessities. Otherwise, we push people into debt or make them suffer by choosing between heating or eating, or indeed contribute to homelessness, both visible and hidden.

Finally, having a minimum wage will give people better access to social goods and services that help them to flourish and live their most productive and enjoyable lives.

The minimum wage in the UK should be raised to a level that is enough to live on.  This should be matched with price controls on essentials, such as rent, electricity (if it is to remain a private good) & heating.  Only then will people see a benefit to the increase.  The increase should be gradual to allow the economy to adjust.  The increase should be accompanied by a tax on the highest earners to ensure that the increase is not funded by those who can least afford it.

The minimum wage in the UK should be raised to a level that is enough to live on.  This should be accompanied by a tax on the highest earners to ensure that the increase is not funded by those who can least afford it.  The increase should be gradual to allow the economy to adjust.  The increase should not be accompanied by price controls on essentials, as these would need to be regularly reviewed and would not be conducive to a market economy.  There are a number of essential items that people could live without in hard times if need be, but it is harder to survive without basic needs such as heating.  This needs to be considered in cases where essentials become too expensive.  The increase should also be accompanied by government support for local initiatives that help to find and improve employment for those on minimum wage and without a job.
